page.title: Portable Power Station or Inverter? The 150 W Car-Socket Limit Decides
page.h1: Portable power station or inverter: which one to buy
page.desc: Portable power station or inverter? A car's lighter socket gives a plug-in inverter about 150 W. Today's prices, wiring and the 1,800 W BLUETTI Elite 100 V2.
page.answer: Short answer. Get a portable power station unless you already own a 12 V battery. A plug-in inverter gets only about 150 W from a car's lighter socket, and anything near 1,000 W needs battery cables and a 150 A fuse. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 gives 1,800 W from its own 1,024 Wh, no wiring.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Building the inverter route from nothing costs about the same as a power station. Vatrer 1000 W inverter + Vatrer 12V 100Ah battery + Redodo 20 A charger: $129.99 + $259.99 + $82.99 = $472.97, against $499 for the Elite 100 V2. Cables, fuse and a battery box are extra.
  • The kit stores more energy per dollar. $472.97 ÷ 1,280 Wh = $0.37 per Wh, against $499 ÷ 1,024 Wh = $0.49 per Wh. At the outlet, the kit gives 1,280 Wh × 0.90 = 1,152 Wh at the 90% efficiency Xantrex rates its PROwatt SW at (Vatrer gives no figure). That is $0.41 per usable Wh. The Elite 100 V2 gave 890 Wh (OutdoorGearLab), which is $0.56 per Wh, and 946 Wh at a steady 500 W (Techreviewer.de), which is $0.53 per Wh.
  • The power station puts out more. 1,800 W − 1,000 W = 800 W more continuous AC from the Elite 100 V2. It also switches over in 10 ms or less if you use it as a UPS (backup supply).
  • If you already own the battery, the inverter wins clearly. $499 − $129.99 = $369.01 saved by buying only the Vatrer inverter.
  • Size the inverter to the battery. A 150 A BMS (battery management system) × 12.8 V = 1,920 W for the Vatrer battery. On that battery alone, a 2,000 W inverter asks for more current than the BMS allows.
  • Recharging in the car is slow through the socket. 1,024 Wh ÷ about 100 W ≈ 10 h. BLUETTI says its 560 W Charger 1 refills a 1 kWh station in 2.5 h.

Why a car's lighter socket changes the answer

An inverter makes no power of its own. In a car it draws from the 12 V system, and the lighter socket is the weak link. Cobra's CPI 400 manual says: "Do not use the cigarette cord for loads higher than 150 watts." Above that, it says a direct connection to the battery is recommended. That limits a 400 W inverter to less than half its rating when it is plugged in. The Directed VDC301 manual explains why: "Most cigarette lighter currents are fused between 10-15 amps". That works out to 10–15 A × 12 V = 120–180 W before conversion losses. The same manual says to connect directly to the power source above 100 W.

A real 1,000 W-class inverter therefore has no plug at all. The Xantrex PROwatt SW 1000 is hardwire-only and is rated 900 W continuous and 2,000 W peak. Xantrex recommends a 150 A DC fuse and lists under 0.6 A no-load draw and 90% efficiency. At 900 W ÷ 12 V ≈ 75 A, it pulls five to seven times what a lighter-socket fuse allows, and it draws that from the car's own battery.

A power station turns this around. Its 1,800 W comes from its own battery, so the car socket doesn't limit what it can run. The socket only limits how fast it refills: BLUETTI's Charger 1 FAQ says "a standard cigarette lighter port in a 12V vehicle outputs around 100W". That is why BLUETTI sells the 560 W Charger 1, which wires to the car battery and charges from the alternator while the engine runs. If you take one box to a campsite and refill it at home, the Elite 100 V2 needs no car wiring at all: {buy:bluetti-elite-100-v2}.

Not recommended

The Sun Gold Power 2000W 12V inverter/charger is $657 on Sun Gold's store, and both its new and refurbished versions were sold out on 2026-11-13. Sun Gold lists 28 W idle draw (13 W in power-saver mode). 1,280 Wh ÷ 28 W ≈ 46 h, so with nothing plugged in it empties a 1,280 Wh battery such as the Vatrer 12V 100Ah in under two days. Its 2,000 W rating is also more than the Vatrer battery's 150 A BMS can feed (1,920 W).
